The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. A **finite reversible stochastic rate model** consists of an integer $r\ge2$, the finite state set $E=\{1,\ldots,r\}$, real energy parameters $e_a\in\mathbb R$, an inverse-energy parameter $\beta>0$, and finite transition rates $w_{ab}\ge0$ for distinct $a,b\in E$. When physical units are assigned, $e_a$ is measured in joules, $\beta$ in joules$^{-1}$, and $w_{ab}$ in seconds$^{-1}$; this mathematical definition does not assert a physical realization. Define

$$Z:=\sum_{a\in E}e^{-\beta e_a},\qquad \pi_a:=Z^{-1}e^{-\beta e_a}.$$

Then $Z$ is finite and positive, and $\pi$ is a strictly positive probability vector. Require $w_{ab}>0$ exactly when $w_{ba}>0$, require the undirected graph with edge $\{a,b\}$ whenever $w_{ab}>0$ to be connected, and impose detailed balance $\pi_aw_{ab}=\pi_bw_{ba}$. Define the row generator $Q$ by $Q_{ab}=w_{ab}$ for $a\ne b$ and $Q_{aa}=-q_a$, where $q_a:=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}$. Since $r\ge2$ and the graph is connected, every $q_a>0$. Thus $(Qf)_a=\sum_{b\ne a}w_{ab}(f_b-f_a)$ for a column observable $f$, and a row probability vector evolves by $p'=pQ$.

For any observable $f:E\to\mathbb R$, write $\pi(f):=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_a$. For $f,g:E\to\mathbb R$, define $\langle f,g\rangle_\pi:=\sum_{a\in E}\pi_af_ag_a$. Since $E$ is finite and every $\pi_a>0$, all real functions on $E$ belong to this finite-dimensional real inner-product space, denoted $L^2(E,\pi)$; equality in it is pointwise equality.

The associated jump-chain construction waits an exponential time of rate $q_a$ in state $a$ and then selects state $b\ne a$ with probability $w_{ab}/q_a$, using fresh independent random choices at successive jumps. Here an exponential time of rate $q>0$ has survival probability $\Pr(\tau>t)=e^{-qt}$ for $t\ge0$. The Ionescu–Tulcea construction [[thm-ionescu-tulcea-construction-of-a-markov-chain]] supplies the countable random sequence under the stated Choice assumption. The theorem on this page proves nonexplosion, identifies the transition semigroup, and establishes the positive reversible spectral gap. This is a finite mathematical rate model, not a derivation of rates from Hamiltonian mechanics.

Assume Choice. Let $(E_n,\mathcal E_n)_{n\ge0}$ be measurable spaces, let
$\mu_0$ be a probability measure on $E_0$, and, for each $n\ge0$, let $K_n$ be
a probability kernel from $E_0\times\cdots\times E_n$ to $E_{n+1}$. There is a
unique probability measure $P$ on
$$ \left(\prod_{n\ge0}E_n,\ \bigotimes_{n\ge0}\mathcal E_n\right) $$ whose finite-prefix laws are the prescribed iterated integrals $$ \mu_0(dx_0)K_0(x_0,dx_1)K_1(x_0,x_1,dx_2)\cdots K_{r-1}(x_0,\ldots,x_{r-1},dx_r). $$
In particular, if every $E_n=E$ and
$K_n(x_0,\ldots,x_n,A)=K(x_n,A)$, the coordinate process is a homogeneous
$K$-chain with initial law $\mu_0$.

Let $V$ be a finite-dimensional real inner product space and let $T:V\to V$ be
self-adjoint. Then $V$ has an orthonormal basis consisting of eigenvectors of
$T$.

derivations.claim: Set $\Lambda>\max_aq_a$ and $K:=I+Q/\Lambda$. Every off-diagonal entry of $K$ is nonnegative, $K_{aa}=1-q_a/\Lambda>0$, and each row sums to one, so $K$ is a transition matrix. The balance relation in [F1] gives $\pi_aK_{ab}=\pi_bK_{ba}$ for all $a,b$. Use [F2] with state space $E\times(0,1)$, initial state distributed as $p_0$ with an independent uniform mark, and transition kernel $K(a,b)\,du'$ from $(a,u)$ to $(b,u')$. Write $Y_n$ for the state coordinate and $U_n$ for the uniform mark; the sequence $Y_n$ has transitions $K$, and the marks $U_n$ are independent uniforms independent of the state sequence. The holding intervals $\tau_n:=-\log U_n/\Lambda$ are independent exponentials of rate $\Lambda$.

For every $n$, $\Pr(\tau_n\ge1/\Lambda)=e^{-1}$. For each fixed $m$, independence gives probability $(1-e^{-1})^N$ that none of $\tau_m,\ldots,\tau_{m+N-1}$ reaches $1/\Lambda$; this tends to zero. A countable union over $m$ shows that infinitely many holding intervals are at least $1/\Lambda$, almost surely. Therefore $S_n:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\tau_j\to\infty$. For each $t\ge0$, there is a unique $N(t)$ with $S_{N(t)}\le t<S_{N(t)+1}$; set $X_t:=Y_{N(t)}$. Thus the constructed path is piecewise constant and has only finitely many transition attempts on each bounded interval. This proves nonexplosion.

The sum of $k\ge1$ independent rate-$\Lambda$ exponential holding times has density $\Lambda^ks^{k-1}e^{-\Lambda s}/(k-1)!$, as follows by induction using convolution. Integrating this density against the survival $e^{-\Lambda(t-s)}$ of the next holding time gives $\Pr(N(t)=k)=e^{-\Lambda t}(\Lambda t)^k/k!$; for $k=0$ it is $e^{-\Lambda t}$. Starting from state $a$, each uniformized attempt stays at $a$ with probability $K_{aa}=1-q_a/\Lambda$. Since $N(t)$ is Poisson and independent of the $K$-chain, the probability of no state change by time $t$ is $\sum_{k\ge0}e^{-\Lambda t}(\Lambda t)^kK_{aa}^k/k!=e^{-q_at}$. At the first attempt that changes state, the destination $b
e a$ has conditional probability $K_{ab}/(1-K_{aa})=w_{ab}/q_a$. Thus the actual holding time and jump destination have exactly the law stated in the Definition. The exponential holding times are memoryless and independent of the $K$-chain, so after any time the remaining clock and future transitions have the same laws from the current state; conditioning on $N(t)$ therefore yields the time-homogeneous transition matrix $P_t=e^{-\Lambda t}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}(\Lambda t)^kK^k/k!=e^{tQ}$ because $Q=\Lambda(K-I)$. The finite-matrix series converges absolutely, differentiates termwise, and satisfies $P'_t=P_tQ$ and $P_0=I$. Each term is stochastic, hence $P_t$ is stochastic. For each state $b$, detailed balance gives $(\pi Q)_b=\sum_{a
e b}\pi_aw_{ab}-\pi_bq_b=\pi_b\sum_{a
e b}w_{ba}-\pi_b\sum_{a
e b}w_{ba}=0$; therefore $\pi P_t=\pi$.

For $f,g\in L^2(E,\pi)$, detailed balance gives $\langle f,Qg\rangle_\pi=\langle Qf,g\rangle_\pi$. Pairing the two directed terms for each edge gives $-\langle f,Qf\rangle_\pi=\frac12\sum_{a\in E}\sum_{b\ne a}\pi_aw_{ab}(f_b-f_a)^2\ge0$. Equality holds only when $f_a=f_b$ along every positive-rate edge; connectedness in [F1] then makes $f$ constant. Thus the zero eigenspace is exactly the constants. By [F3], $Q$ has a real orthonormal eigenbasis; nonpositivity and the one-dimensional kernel imply all other eigenvalues are $-\lambda_j$ with $\lambda_j>0$. Expanding in this basis gives $P_tf=\pi(f)1+\sum_{j=1}^{r-1}e^{-\lambda_jt}\langle f,\phi_j\rangle_\pi\phi_j$, proving the positive gap and exponential convergence.

Apply [F2] on $((E\times(0,1))^2)$ with initial state whose two $E$ coordinates are equal with law $\pi$ and whose two marks $U_0^+,U_0^-$ are independent uniforms. From a state pair $(a^+,a^-)$, use the product kernel $K(a^+,b^+)K(a^-,b^-)\,du'^+du'^-$; this makes the two $K$-chains conditionally independent given their shared initial state and gives independent uniform marks at every step. Denote the state coordinates by $Y_n^\pm$, set $\tau_n^\pm:=-\log U_n^\pm/\Lambda$, $S_0^\pm:=0$, and $S_n^\pm:=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\tau_j^\pm$. For $s\ge0$, let $N^\pm(s)$ be the unique index with $S_{N^\pm(s)}^\pm\le s<S_{N^\pm(s)+1}^\pm$ and put $Z_s^\pm:=Y_{N^\pm(s)}^\pm$. Step 2.1 applied to each clock sequence ensures these indices exist for every finite $s$. Put $X_t=Z_t^+$ for $t\ge0$ and $X_t=Z_{-t}^-$ for $t<0$. For times entirely on the nonnegative half, the Markov-chain law has the stated product form. For negative times $t_1<\cdots<t_k<0$, append the time $0$ with state $c=X_0$. In the forward parameter $s=-t$, the ordered states are $c,a_k,\ldots,a_1$, so their joint probability is $\pi_cP_{-t_k}(c,a_k)\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_{i+1},a_i)$. Applying $\pi_aP_u(a,b)=\pi_bP_u(b,a)$ first to the factor from $0$ to $t_k$ and then successively to the remaining factors gives $\pi_{a_1}\prod_{i=1}^{k-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})P_{-t_k}(a_k,c)$. Summing over $c$ gives the negative-time marginal; $k=1$ is included by the empty-product convention. If a list also has nonnegative times, conditional independence of the halves given $X_0=c$ multiplies this negative-side factor by $P_{t_{k+1}}(c,a_{k+1})\prod_{i=k+1}^{n-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})$. For adjacent times $t_k<0\le t_{k+1}$ around zero, summing over $c$ joins the two factors because $\sum_cP_{-t_k}(a_k,c)P_{t_{k+1}}(c,a_{k+1})=P_{t_{k+1}-t_k}(a_k,a_{k+1})$, by the semigroup law. Thus in every case the joint probability is $\pi_{a_1}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}P_{t_{i+1}-t_i}(a_i,a_{i+1})$, which depends only on time differences. For each $a\in E$, the set $\{(s,\omega):Z_s^\pm(\omega)=a\}$ equals $\bigcup_{n\ge0}\{(s,\omega):S_n^\pm(\omega)\le s<S_{n+1}^\pm(\omega),\ Y_n^\pm(\omega)=a\}$; every set in this union is product-measurable because $S_n^\pm$ and $Y_n^\pm$ are measurable. Since $E$ is finite, both half-processes are jointly measurable, and composing the negative half with $t\mapsto -t$ and gluing on the measurable half-lines preserves joint measurability. Step 2.1 gives finitely many jumps on every bounded interval on both halves, so the glued process has the stated local path property.

> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0},P)$ carry a standard Brownian motion $B$ adapted to the filtration, with future increments independent of the present sigma-algebra. Fix constants $\gamma>0$ and $\sigma>0$, and an $\mathcal F_0$-measurable real random variable $X_0$ with finite second moment. A **continuous adapted solution of the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck equation** on $[0,T]$ is a continuous adapted process $X$ satisfying, almost surely for every $t\in[0,T]$,
$$X_t=X_0-\gamma\int_0^tX_s\,ds+\sigma B_t,$$
where the time integral is the ordinary Lebesgue integral along the continuous path. In differential notation this is $dX_t=-\gamma X_t\,dt+\sigma\,dB_t$, with the stochastic differential interpreted through the displayed integral equation.

The definition asserts neither existence nor uniqueness. The Itô integral in the explicit representation is the square-integrable predictable-process integral of [[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]].

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Assume the filtered probability space, Brownian increment hypothesis, and initial data of [[def-tdmath-ornstein-uhlenbeck-equation]], including $\mathbb E X_0^2<\infty$ and future increments independent of $\mathcal F_0$. For $\gamma,\sigma>0$, on every finite time interval the process
$$X_t=e^{-\gamma t}X_0+\sigma e^{-\gamma t}\int_0^t e^{\gamma s}\,dB_s$$
has a continuous adapted version, solves the stated Ornstein–Uhlenbeck integral equation, and is the unique continuous solution driven by the same $(X_0,B)$. Put $V=\sigma^2/(2\gamma)$. For $0\le s<t$, its transition law conditional on $\mathcal F_s$ is normal with mean $e^{-\gamma(t-s)}X_s$ and variance $V(1-e^{-2\gamma(t-s)})$. Consequently
$$\mathbb E X_t=e^{-\gamma t}\mathbb E X_0,\qquad\operatorname{Var}(X_t)=e^{-2\gamma t}\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+V(1-e^{-2\gamma t}).$$
From any such initial law, $X_t$ converges in distribution to $N(0,V)$. If $X_0\sim N(0,V)$ and is independent of future Brownian increments, the process is stationary Gaussian with covariance $C(\tau)=Ve^{-\gamma|\tau|}$, and its transition kernel satisfies detailed balance with the $N(0,V)$ density. Its transition density solves the Fokker–Planck equation for positive time. Under the convention $S(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1}\int_{\mathbb R}C(\tau)e^{i\omega\tau}\,d\tau$, the stationary spectrum and time-average bound are
$$S(\omega)=\frac{V\gamma}{\pi(\gamma^2+\omega^2)},\qquad\operatorname{Var}\!\left(\frac1T\int_0^T X_t\,dt\right)\le\frac{2V}{\gamma T}.$$
All these statements concern the specified linear stochastic model. An Einstein relation between $\sigma$ and a physical bath temperature would be an additional physical postulate.

derivations.claim: Let $V^0$ be the unforced OU solution from [F2], satisfying the integral equation in [F1]. Define the deterministic function $g(t):=\frac1m\int_0^te^{-\gamma(t-s)}u(s)\,ds$. Differentiation under this finite integral gives $g(0)=0$ and $g'(t)=-\gamma g(t)+u(t)/m$, hence $g(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tg(s)\,ds+\frac1m\int_0^tu(s)\,ds$. Adding this identity to the unforced equation shows that the continuous adapted process $V_t:=V^0_t+g(t)$ satisfies $V_t=V_0-\gamma\int_0^tV_s\,ds+\frac1m\int_0^tu(s)\,ds+\sigma B_t$, the forced equation in the Statement. If two forced solutions have the same initial state and Brownian path, their difference $z$ satisfies $z(t)=-\gamma\int_0^tz(s)\,ds$; with $H(t)=\int_0^t|z(s)|\,ds$, one has $H'(t)\le\gamma H(t)$ and $H(0)=0$. Thus $(e^{-\gamma t}H(t))'\le0$, so $H=0$ and $z=0$. Uniqueness makes the finite-horizon solutions agree on overlaps; gluing along integer horizons gives the solution for all $t\ge0$ on a common probability-one event.

Since $V^0$ is centered and $g$ is deterministic, $\mathbb E V_t=g(t)$, giving the claimed mean. The parameter relation gives $\sigma^2/(2\gamma)=k_B\Theta/m=v_\Theta$, so [F2] gives stationarity, Gaussianity and the displayed covariance for the unforced solution.

For a uniform partition of $[0,t]$, the Riemann sums $S_n=(t/n)\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}V_{jt/n}$ converge almost surely to $Y_t$ because $V$ has continuous paths. Each $S_n$ is centered Gaussian under $u=0$. By the covariance in step 2.1, its variance is a Riemann sum converging to $\int_0^t\int_0^t v_\Theta e^{-\gamma|s-r|}\,ds\,dr=2v_\Theta\int_0^t(t-a)e^{-\gamma a}\,da=2v_\Theta\left(\frac{t}{\gamma}-\frac{1-e^{-\gamma t}}{\gamma^2}\right)$. Hence the Gaussian characteristic functions of $S_n$ converge to that of the centered normal with this variance. For each real $\xi$, almost-sure convergence and $|e^{i\xi S_n}|=1$ let bounded convergence give $\mathbb E e^{i\xi S_n}\to\mathbb E e^{i\xi Y_t}$. Therefore $Y_t$ has the stated Gaussian law and variance. Adding the deterministic $g$ to velocity changes only the mean of its integral, not this variance.

Dividing the variance formula in step 3.1 by $2t$ and letting $t\to\infty$ gives $D=v_\Theta/\gamma$. The centered displacement has Gaussian variance $2Dt-2v_\Theta(1-e^{-\gamma t})/\gamma^2$; after division by $t$ this tends to $2D$, proving the distributional limit. For constant $u_0$, step 1.1 gives $\mathbb E V_t=u_0(1-e^{-\gamma t})/(m\gamma)$, so $\chi=1/(m\gamma)$ and $D=(k_B\Theta/m)/\gamma=\chi k_B\Theta$.

Starting with observed block $C_1$, [F2] gives $\Pr_1(\bar X_h=C_2)=O(h^2)$ and $\Pr_2(\bar X_h=C_2)=h+O(h^2)$, because a transition from $1$ to $3$ needs at least two jumps, while the direct $2\to3$ rate is $1$. The two preparations have the same initial block but different first-order block-transition probabilities.

Therefore no single transition law on $\{C_1,C_2\}$ can govern the projection for both microscopic preparations. Equivalently, the required block-rate constancy in [F3] fails. This refutes the universal all-preparations claim; it makes no assertion about special initial preparations.
